To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The overall importance of risk factors in the population is determined not by the risk factor's relative risk (RR), but by the product of the RR and the prevalence of the factor in the population (the population attributable risk, PAR).
the population attributable risk of suicide for low SES factors is comparable with the population attributable risk for psychiatric risk factors.
the attributable risk of suicide associated with socio-economic status was similar in magnitude to psychiatric disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prevention of suicide, which has been identified as a global health priority.
understanding the role of mental health and socioeconomic status (SES) as risk factors for suicide.
the development of a new approach to the study of suicide.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the PAR of suicide is high for both psychiatric disorders and low SES, with the relative ranking of the two risk factors being dependent on gender and the particular disorder and SES measure considered.
suicide prevention strategies which target lower SES groups may have similar population level effects as those targeting mental disorder.
the most important factors in the etiology of suicide are the same as for the etiology of mental disorders, namely mental disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the most important factor in suicide is socio-economic deprivation.
suicide risk is associated with both socio-economic deprivation and mental disorders.
suicide prevention strategies which focus only on mental disorders may not have the same population-level effect as those which focus on socio-economic deprivation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a range of risk factors that can be used to prevent suicide.
suicide is a preventable disease.
there are two major domains that have been studied with regard to suicide, and that the two domains have very similar population attributable risks.
